wa_prusik_peak_prayer_for_a_friend.notes: Start in the obvious easy corner just left of Der Sportsman. Ramble up slabby ground in the corner, pulling over a few small roofs, to a two-bolt belay. The route then cuts right to head straight for the base of the summit headwall.
Move up and left to a band of overlapping flakes and roofs, step out onto the face, and undercling across into a secure stemming box. Belay there on two offset bolts.
Climb the corner to a short, awkward flare that holds the crux of the pitch, then continue to a two-bolt anchor. The flare is technical rather than strenuous.

Follow the obvious hand crack until you can step right to a bolt, then climb past suspect rock to a second bolt. The hardest climbing passes the next two bolts to easier ground. A blue Totem or a 0.3–0.4 offset cam is useful. Belay on the ledge at a two-bolt anchor.

Clip the first bolt, move left to cam placements, then work up a series of left-leaning seams. The moves are tricky rather than desperate, but the rock is poorer than on the pitches below, so test holds and place gear carefully.

The headwall: 5.11+ liebacking on imperfect rock to a bolt and a shake-out crimp, then a step right into a slightly overhanging finger splitter. About twenty hard, sequential moves on sloping locks follow, with only a few gear placements, before easier stemming. Belay on a single bolt backed up with a small cam; the pitch ends on the West Ridge.

The route ends on the West Ridge short of the top. Scramble the remaining ridge to the summit, then descend by the West Ridge rappels. The headwall pitch can also be reached by climbing the West Ridge and rappelling in to it.

wa_the_scoop_2.notes: A bouldery move off the ground leads to easier terrain and a belay at a small, rotting tree.
Climb into a groove; demanding moves trend right to easier ground and a tree belay.
Crux moves up a dihedral, then a short slab to 'Launch Ledge' — relocate the belay about 30 feet left before starting the Scoop pitch.
'The Scoop' pitch: a crack into a corner, then sustained finger-and-hand jamming up the giant scooped dihedral to a hand-crack finish. 'Nectar' (5.10+) bypasses the crux to the right.
Traverse a small ledge into a slab dihedral with thin, tricky protection through a small roof.
Climb the right side, traverse left to a rock tooth, then a 5.9 dihedral to the final technical belay ledge.
Simulclimb easy 4th/5th-class terrain toward the summit block.
Continue simulclimbing broken, low-angle rock; no fixed gear anywhere on this route by design.
Easy blocky terrain toward the base of the summit block; natural anchors (trees, horns) throughout.
The exposed final boulder problem to the top of the balanced summit block; parties commonly fix a toprope for the second.

wa_the_tipping_point.notes: Climb the corner using a variety of techniques; the crux is getting off the ground, with a second hard section mid-pitch. Two-bolt belay.
Traverse left past bolts with tricky knob wrangling, then layback past more bolts to a two-bolt belay.

Climb a seam, make the crux move to gain the crack (the 'flower power crack') on very small gear, then power up the corner to the Sky Lounge — a stellar ledge with two bolts. This is the natural bail point.

The crux. Traverse right, climb featured slab, punch through an overhanging gold-rock flare, follow the crack to a roof, traverse left, then solve a final boulder problem. Kerwin's Crack (5.12/12+) links into this crux as a harder variation.
Hand and finger crack climbing to a sandy alcove belay. End of the route's independent climbing.
Joins Let it Burn: a thin corner feature leading to lower-angled slabs and a slab belay.
Let it Burn continued: face and knob climbing to a crack in an alcove, then out the left edge of a roof.
Blocky terrain and right-leaning cracks to the summit area; the true top-out is a short V1 boulder problem on the balanced summit block, which most parties protect with a rope.

wy_irene_s_arete.notes: Starts at a tree well to the right of the arete proper. Easy, straightforward climbing leads to a good block stance. Parties traversing in from the Caves side rarely see the tree and rope up about 40 ft above it; make an intermediate belay there, because a flake catches the rope and makes belaying the second to the next start awkward.

The most sustained and serious pitch. The line is flaring and partly off-width. An old piton sits at the crux bulge but only protects once the move is made, so back it up with a small cam (about a 0.75) and be solid. The belay is a huge ledge. It is possible to escape right from here with two rappels (a 60 m rope was used; a 50 m rope may not reach without leaving gear).

The original line crosses back and forth over the arete on a roofy pitch through a black rock band, starting just left of the arete on a runout but easy face before returning to the right side. Fun face climbing with roof pulls that finishes at a good belay ledge. A committing 5.9 variant goes right off the ledge and works back left into the black band.

Traverse left; gear is available before moving around the arete, but a second's fall on the traverse swings out and off the arete. Then climb good holds up through the black rock and traverse back right across quartz on a delicate sequence of footholds. A fixed piece on the traverse is worn and worth backing up with a cam. The belay is on a sloping ledge, using a fixed pin plus gear in a seam. A sustained 5.8 variant stays right of the arete.

Climb cracks and face moves left of the sloping ledge to a horizontal knife-edge. Straight ahead of the belay, a steeper 5.9 crack running from fingers to hands cuts a short band of quartz, with jugs to help through an off-balance move and big exposure below. From the knife-edge, a short leapfrog gets you to a tree.

The standard way goes down and right roughly 150 ft into a gully and then up a weakness (about 5.5). The more direct line is a 5.8 hand and fist crack in front of the tree, with sustained fist jams and poor feet. A 5.9+ to 5.10a variant takes the arete crest more directly on the left, and a 5.9 option stays left of the arete. Belay on an easy slab.
Easy ground for a couple of hundred feet up and left, then back right. Soloing, simul-climbing or belaying all work. The walk-off appears obvious on the right.

ut_fine_jade.notes: The most physical pitch. An off-width that narrows to fists climbs over a bulge, then a thin, strenuous hand crack slants right to a little roof. Over the roof is a brief wide stretch, then a hand crack closing down to fingers ends at a bolted belay on a ledge.
Jam past a bulge into a finger crack, move right into a wider section, then take a hand crack that narrows to fingers up to a ledge with three bolts. It is often linked with pitch 1.

The hardest moves. Move right and jam thin cracks up to a horizontal, then a long finger crack to a pod; from there finger and hand cracks lead left over two small bulges to a ledge belay on two bolts. A 0.5-size cam is the awkward size to have here.
A corner and a series of ledges trend right over somewhat sandy rock, then the line returns left to a roomy ledge with two bolts. A bolt protects the second.

Two finishes. The regular left finish climbs a short corner, hand-traverses left to an off-width in a dihedral, then traverses left under a roof (about 5.7 and airy) to the summit. Use plenty of slings against rope drag, or split the pitch in two. The direct right finish climbs the corner and then face moves past four bolts at 5.11a.
